I am fifty-nine years old, and I have never been to school. I cannot read or write, but I know this land because my father taught me, and I have farmed these fields for over forty years. I have seven mu of land in Quzhou, and I do what every farmer around here does: wheat in the winter, corn in the summer. That is the only way that makes sense. The wheat went into the ground last October before the frost came. Now it is waking up, so I will topdress it with compound fertilizer—about eighty jin per mu, the kind the shopkeeper says is good for wheat, with plenty of nitrogen and phosphorus. I will water it four times from my well: the green-up water, the jointing water, the heading water, and one more if the weather turns dry. When I see aphids or rust, I spray. I use the rotary tiller before planting, always have.

After I cut the wheat in early June, I will plant summer corn the same day or the next. No need to plough—just put the seeds straight into the stubble. I buy hybrid corn seed from the shop, one bag per mu. The corn needs less water, maybe two good irrigations, and I spray twice for bugs. I expect about one thousand jin of wheat per mu, and a bit more for the corn, maybe eleven hundred jin per mu, if the weather cooperates. I do not try new crops or fancy tricks. I follow what works, what my neighbors do, and what I have always done.
